summary: Millbrae sits directly atop a BART and Caltrain intermodal station — one of only two in the entire Bay Area — which means a single platform connects you to both San Francisco and San Jose without touching a car, a fact that quietly shapes the entire city's real estate gravity. At just 3.3 square miles, it's compact enough to walk from the hillside residential streets west of El Camino Real down to the bayfront flats, gaining or losing a couple hundred feet of elevation along the way; those upper-slope homes often catch unobstructed views across the San Francisco Bay toward the East Bay hills. The proximity to SFO — the airport is literally next door — delivers obvious commute advantages for travel-heavy industries but also delivers occasional jet noise on certain approach paths, a tradeoff baked into the geography. A median home price north of $1.9 million against a median household income around $158K yields a price-to-income ratio above 12:1, meaning even upper-middle earnings face steep math on a purchase. Daily highs averaging 65°F year-round with minimal temperature swings create that classic Peninsula microclimate — cool enough for a jacket most evenings, rarely hot enough for air conditioning. Millbrae is fundamentally a residential city with extraordinary transit bones, where the defining tension is between that connectivity premium and the cost of claiming it.
